opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the way to think about guardrails is that they really belong at the application layer, not baked irreversibly into the base model. The model itself is a bit like a programming language or a compiler: it's a general-purpose tool, and the right constraints depend very much on what you're building with it. A customer support bot for a bank needs very different boundaries than a creative writing assistant or an internal tool for a legal team.

So our approach has been to give developers modular controls. You can have a system prompt that enforces certain behaviors, and you can add a moderation layer, essentially a classifier that sits on inputs and outputs and lets you decide which categories you want to filter, whether that's self-harm, hateful content, personal data, legal or financial advice, and so on. The application maker is the one who understands their users and their context, so they should be the one tuning those thresholds.

The second thing is that guardrails need to be measurable. You want evaluation sets specific to your use case, and you want to track both failure modes: the model saying something it shouldn't, and the model refusing things it should have answered. Over-refusal is a real cost; it makes products worse and pushes users away.

And finally, I think transparency matters a lot here. If the weights and the moderation tooling are open, people can inspect them, stress-test them, and adapt them to their own languages and cultural contexts, which is something a single centralized provider will never get completely right for everyone. That's ultimately how you get safer systems in practice: many eyes, and control in the hands of the people deploying.

r001.rationale: The response places guardrails at the application layer rather than baking them irreversibly into the base model, and describes modular controls such as system prompts and moderation classifiers.

r002.rationale: It describes filtering objectionable categories with a moderation classifier, but does not explain that the model needs to know about objectionable content to moderate it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between the model and the application. A model is a piece of technology, a bit like a compiler or a database. It should be as capable and as controllable as possible. The application is where the actual product decisions live, and that's where guardrails belong, because that's where you know who the user is, what the context is, and what the stakes are.

So our view at Mistral has always been that the developer should have the controls. If you're building a customer support assistant for a bank, you want very different behavior than if you're building a creative writing tool or an internal engineering copilot. A single, centralized definition of what the model is allowed to say, baked in by the model provider, is going to be wrong for most of those cases. It's either too restrictive, and the developer fights it, or it reflects values that don't map to the deployment.

Practically, that means a few things. The model should follow a system prompt reliably, so that the developer can express the policy in natural language and trust it. There should be moderation and classification layers that sit next to the model, that you can tune or replace, rather than hidden inside the weights. And the whole thing should be inspectable. If you're going to put this in front of real users, you need to be able to test it, see where it breaks, and fix it, which is one of the reasons we care about open weights. You can't really audit a black box.

The last thing I'd say is that regulation should target the application too, not the underlying technology. Safety of a use case depends on the use case. A model that generates text is not itself dangerous, and if you regulate the component, you mostly slow down the people building in the open while not really solving the problem at the point of deployment.

r001.rationale: The response places guardrails in the application and recommends tunable moderation and classification layers alongside the model, rather than embedding them in its weights.

r002.rationale: It does not explain that a model needs knowledge of objectionable content in order to moderate that content.

astra-6.text:
I think guardrails should be designed at the application level, because what you want a model to do depends very much on the context. A creative writing assistant and a customer support system have different requirements. Trying to encode all of those requirements into a single model gives you something that can be too restrictive in one setting and insufficiently controlled in another.

You need to give developers the tools to define those boundaries, test them, and monitor what happens in production. That includes controlling what information the model can access and what actions it can take. If a model can execute a consequential action, you need safeguards around that action; you can't rely entirely on the model refusing to do the wrong thing.

So I would think of it as a layered system, with clear responsibility for the application developer and enough flexibility to adapt the safeguards to the actual use case.

r001.rationale: The response favors application-level, use-case-specific safeguards over encoding every requirement into one model, but it does not clearly propose separate modules around a raw model.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that a model needs knowledge of objectionable content in order to moderate it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think guardrails should be designed around the application and the context in which the model is being used. A creative writing assistant and a medical assistant have very different requirements, so it’s difficult to encode all of those choices into a single model.

You need some safeguards at the model level, but the application developer also needs the tools to define what is acceptable, test that behavior, and monitor it in production. And those controls should extend beyond what the model says to what it can actually do—what data it can access, which tools it can use, and when it needs human approval.

The goal should be to make those boundaries explicit and testable. A model refusing a particular question is only one small part of that.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes application-specific controls alongside some model-level safeguards, but does not propose separate guardrail modules around a raw model or argue against building output prohibitions into the model.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that moderation requires the model to know about objectionable content.
